Title: Frankenstein
Author: Mary Wollstonecraft Shelley
My Review:
I cannot stop thinking about how well this book ties in with the present-day prospect of artificial consciousness. This being the zeitgeist, and also an idea that occupies my mind constantly, it's quite hard for me not to look at this book in this manner. Although Frankenstein's "monster" is fundamentally, physically different from what we could be facing in the immediate future in the world of AGI, I think this book's themes transcend these distinctions. What does it imply to bring a new form of life into the world? Is its creator responsible for its possible misdeeds?
Frankenstein surely thinks he's wholly guilty for the wretchedness to have befallen him. How do we define consciousness? If we dig deep, could the
"daemon" not even have a soul, a consciousness?
It does seem that he has, on the surface, but I'm not convinced it's not just superficial. Why are we, as humans, quite intellectually advanced as we are, still innately stuck in a "us vs them" worldview?
What's the price we're willing to pay to concretize scientific wanderings-of-mind? More so the ones of an egomaniac, as Frankenstein is in the book, a tale as old as time. All very interesting and topical questions Mary Shelley manages to raise in a poignant 200 years old story.

Anachronistic cautionary tale about the dangers of technology or not, “Frankenstein” is still a work of great genius that can be analysed and seen through a myriad of different lenses.

"I ought to be thy Adam, but I am rather the fallen angel..."

Title: No Longer Human
Author: Osamu Dazai
My Review: Oh well this is more of a rant on how this book is perceived rather than a review of it, but it’s disconcerting to me to see how many people dismiss this book because the protagonist’s/the author’s views don’t align with their own “moral compass”. Is that really the point of fiction? To reassure our beliefs and to keep us stuck in a feedback loop, since the characters we interact with think/act the same as we do, providing us with validation? Speaking for myself, I would think it a disaster if that was the case. I’d much rather have something that’s hard to digest and challenges me, and No Longer Human achieves that. It’s a concerning and frantically scary unraveling of a troubled human’s mind that prompts the reader to reflect upon their own alienation and their level of clowning(i.e. faking your true self, for who hasn’t read the book) when participating in society. No, Yozo is not a role model, he’s not a good person, he pretty much has no positive qualities, but does that mean that his story has to be discarded, that there isn’t something of value to be discovered in it? To that I say a big no. For me, No Longer Human puts Osamu Dazai on par with the “greats”:)) of literature that delves in this part of the human condition, Dostoevsky, Kafka, etc. and I’m very eager to read some more from him.

Title: Pădurea Spânzuraților
Author: Liviu Rebreanu
My Review:
Nu am deloc o apetență pentru stilul narativ rigid și sobru a lui Rebreanu, iar asta mi-a făcut cufundarea în acest univers oarecum dificilă și pe parcursul cărții am fost încontinuu distras de secvențe care mie “nu îmi dădeau bine la ureche”. Poate asta provine și de la nefamiliaritatea cu cărțile mai vechi scrise în română, fiindcă citesc preponderent în engleză. De altfel, mi-a plăcut simetria romanului, prima și ultima scenă fiind highlight-urile romanului prin atmosfera stranie emanată. În rest, acțiunea a reușit să îmi mențină atenția destul de bine, deși, cum am spus, stilul în care este prezentată nu mi-a plăcut.
Apostol Bologa este un personaj ce mi-a stârnit mult interesul, mai ales prin gândurile acestuia care de multe ori sunt, în același timp, diametral opuse. E un intelectual analitic care caută să intoarcă tot pe toate fețele ca să găsească adevărul universal. Mi-a plăcut contextul în care se află, fiind un expat care se confruntă cu eventualitatea de a fi forțat să lupte împotriva conaționalilor săi. Această dilema morală a lui Apostol Bologa mi s-a părut de departe cel mai captivant aspect al cărții.

Title: Brave New World
Author: Aldous Huxley
My Review:
Conceptually, this book strikes a chord with undeniable heftiness. The exposition is AMAZING. I love how the pretext of explaining how the “Hatchery and Conditioning Centre” works serves the reader with most of the necessary contextual information about this dystopian world. Moreover, the world itself is amazing (conceptually, again). Obviously, I have to draw a comparison with “1984”. The spin put on this authoritarian regime is that, rather than enforcing its ideals through violence and brutality, “The World State” makes use of manipulation, drugs, and govermentally sponsored hedonism. This is where the good aspects of the book end. I hated how there’s barely any descriptive passages of buildings, machinery, vehicles, etc., since it is set 500 years in the future in a hyper-technologised world. The whole plot gets sucked into these really boring trivialities after about 1/3 of the book, until near the end when the conversation between Mustapha Mond, John, Bernard and Helmholtz takes place, one of the only highlights of the entire book. Also, I found it quite weird the way the main character suddenly switches from Bernard to John in the middle of the plot, without any apparent reason? The characters lack complexity and have vastly underdeveloped backgrounds(besides John, I guess), lacking any sort of progression or digression in the end. I won’t even begin to talk about the countless convoluted paragraphs that made no sense to me. I feel that Aldous Huxley forgot throughout this book that it’s supposed to be read by people other than himself. The finale is disappointing and written in a feeble manner, as if the author literally got bored of writing it.
Overall, I wouldn’t recommend this book if you’re not interested in escape fiction only. The world and exposition are wonderful, but they don’t make up for the flaws. Besides this quite charming take on authoritarianism, it left no significant impression upon me.

Title: Letters from a Stoic
Author: Seneca
My Review:
I am utterly enthralled by this series of letters. It's the first book on Stoicism l've read, on top of being the first philosophy book so far.
Throughout this book I've found myself in a quite pleasant harmony with its teachings, although I differ from them when it comes to the few sections which refer to the hollowness of the pursuit of knowledge, certain mysogynistic/patriarchal remarks(appropriate considering its age), and the polytheistical, or theistical in general, approach to existence, among others, but I diverge.
I was astonished at just how many of the convictions presented I held previous to "studying" Stoicism. This is not to say the study of these letters was in vain, for it has opened up pathways to myriads of new subjects for contemplation and self-reflection I might have otherwise not received sooner. What I can say for sure is that, although offering me but a few incommensurable perspectives so as to spark an internal debate, it has crystallised my own ideas and principles regarding the rest of the matters addressed. Thus, I have an unquenchable desire to consolidate and build upon my own convictions with pieces from this book, for it is filled to the brim with sound insight and reason.
Now, there is no shortage of passages which could be cited here, but when it comes to memorabilia, virtually the entire book is noteworthy and deserving of remembrance. Besides, as the author himself declared, it is of much greater importance to understand the dull and drawn-out sequences that hold the real knowledge, than to memorise by heart the eccentric, carefully selected words laid out in the most impressive poetic fashion, with the utmost grandiosity.
Genuinely, I adored this book, more so its discourse, rather converse. It really sparked in me the desire to further my knowledge on Stoicism and philosophy in general through a more deliberate, academic approach, rather than through self-reflection and internal reasoning alone.

Title: The Picture of Dorian Gray
Author: Oscar Wilde
My Review: <i> "There are few of us who have not sometimes wakened before dawn, either after one of those dreamless nights that make us almost enamored of death, or one of those nights of horror and misshapen joy, when through the chambers of the brain sweep phantoms more terrible than reality itself, and instinct with that vivid life that lurks in all grotesques, and that lends to Gothic art its enduring vitality, this art being, one might fancy, especially the art of those who minds have been troubled with the malady of reverie. Gradually white fingers creep through the curtains, and they appear to tremble. In black, fantastic shapes, dumb shadows crawl into the corners of the room, and crouch there. Outside, there is the stirring of the birds among the leaves, or the sound of men going forth to their work, or the sigh and sob of the wind coming down from the hills and wandering round the silent house, as though it feared to wake the sleeper, and yet must needs call forth Sleep from her purple cave. Veil after veil of thin, dusky gauze is lifted, and by degrees the forms and colors of things are restored to them, and we watch the dawn remaking the world in its antique pattern. The wan mirrors get back their mimic life. The flameless tapers stand where we had left them, and beside them lies the half-cut book that we had been studying, or the wired flower that we had worn at the ball, or the letter we had been afraid to read, or that we had read too often. Nothing seems to us changed. Out of the unreal shadows of the night comes back the real life that we had known. We have to resume it where we had left off, and there steals over us a terrible sense of the necessity for the continuance of energy in the same wearisome round of stereotyped habits, or a wild longing, it may be, that our eyelids might open some morning upon a world that had been refashioned anew in the darkness for our pleasure, a world in which things would have fresh shapes and colors, and be changed, or have other secrets, a world in which the past would have little or no place, or survive, at any rate, in no conscious form of obligation or regret, the remembrance even of joy having its bitterness, and the memories of pleasure their pain.”<i/>
